title: Grable & Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering & Manufacturing (2005)
summary: The quiet-title action belonged in federal court because it necessarily presented a disputed, substantial federal tax issue without disrupting the federal-state allocation of cases.
notes:
The test is conjunctive. Gunn shows that an issue can be necessary and disputed yet lack the required significance to the federal system. Mottley remains the starting rule for locating the issue in the plaintiff’s own claim.

The IRS seized Grable's Michigan property in 1994 for unpaid taxes and sold it to Darue after certified-mail notice; five years later Grable sued to quiet title, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed federal jurisdiction before the Supreme Court (Souter, J., unanimous) did so, clarifying that Merrell Dow's absence of a federal private right of action is a factor, not a bar.

Justice Thomas concurred, suggesting he would be open in a future case to returning to Justice Holmes's test that a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

sections.Parties: Grable, the former owner, sued Darue, the purchaser of property sold after a federal tax seizure.
sections.Material Facts: The Internal Revenue Service seized and sold Grable’s property to satisfy unpaid federal taxes. Grable received notice by certified mail but later asserted that federal law required a different form of personal notice. Years after the sale, it sued to quiet title, arguing that the alleged federal notice defect invalidated Darue’s title. The notice statute’s meaning was thus part of Grable’s own affirmative claim.
sections.Procedural History: Darue removed the state action to federal court. The federal courts sustained jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court affirmed that jurisdictional conclusion.
sections.Issue: Could a state-law quiet-title action arise under federal law when its necessary premise was a disputed interpretation of a federal tax-sale statute?
sections.Holding: Yes. The federal issue was necessarily raised, actually disputed, substantial, and capable of resolution in federal court without disturbing the congressionally approved balance of federal and state responsibilities.
sections.Reasoning: The case turned on the meaning of a federal notice requirement rather than a fact-bound issue with significance only to the parties. The federal government had a strong interest in the reliability and administration of tax sales, including purchasers’ ability to rely on them. At the same time, this kind of federal issue would occur only exceptionally in the ordinary state-law field of quiet-title litigation. Accepting jurisdiction therefore would not move a broad class of routine state disputes into federal court. The absence of a separate federal private cause of action was relevant to congressional design, but it was not an absolute bar to the embedded-issue route.

learning.why: The quiet-title action belonged in federal court because it necessarily presented a disputed, substantial federal tax issue without disrupting the federal-state allocation of cases.

topics.cp-embedded-question: The quiet-title claim necessarily disputed the meaning of the federal tax-sale notice requirement. The federal government’s interest in reliable tax collection made the legal issue important beyond the immediate parties.
topics.cp-federalism: The rarity of this federal issue in quiet-title cases reduced the risk of shifting a large field of state litigation into federal court.
topics.cp-federal-question: Grable defines when a state-law claim arises under federal law for § 1331.
topics.cp-well-pleaded: The federal issue appeared in Grable's own claim, satisfying the well-pleaded complaint rule rather than arising as a defense.
topics.cp-removal: The case reached federal court by Darue's removal, so § 1441 jurisdiction turned on the arising-under analysis.
